5	\subsection{Comparisons Operators}
6	
7	Unless otherwise noted, the operators described in this section
8	produce boolean (\VAR{true}/\VAR{false}) results.
9	
10	The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and $>$ are
11	  used for numerical comparisons
12	and are supported by integer, rational, and floating-point types.
13	Comparison of rational values throws \TYP{RationalComparisonError}
14	if either argument is the rational infinity \EXP{1/0} or the
15	rational indefinite \EXP{0/0}.
16	Comparison of floating-point values throws \TYP{FloatingComparisonError}
17	if either argument is a \TYP{NaN}.
18	
19	The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} may also be
20	used to compare characters
21	(according to the numerical value of their Unicode codepoint values)
22	and strings (lexicographic order based on the character ordering).
23	They also use lexicographic order when used to compare lists
24	whose elements support these same comparison operators.
25	
26	When $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} are used to compare numerical
27	intervals, the result is a boolean interval.  The functions
28	\VAR{possibly} and \VAR{certainly} are useful for converting
29	boolean intervals to boolean values for testing.  Thus
30	\EXP{\VAR{possibly}(x>y)} is true if and only if there is some value in the interval
31	\VAR{x} that is greater than some value in the interval \VAR{y}, while
32	\EXP{\VAR{certainly}(x>y)} is true if and only if \VAR{x} and \VAR{y} are nonempty
33	and every value in \VAR{x} is greater than every value in \VAR{y}.
34	
35	The operators \EXP{\subset}, \EXP{\subseteq}, \EXP{\supseteq}, and
36	\EXP{\supset} may be used to compare sets or intervals regarded as sets.
37	
38	The operator \EXP{\in} may be used to test whether a value is a member of
39	a set, list, array, interval, or range.

46	\begin{description}

56	variables and that ``we could just rule this a special case'', answers

59	instantiation for each type the variable may stand for, and instantiation

=== CondExtendChecker.test
tests=CondExtendChecker
typecheck
=== CondExtendChecker.fss
(* A pair is ordered when its elements are, and a vector adds when its elements do: a conditional extension holds where its condition does, and the declaration's members are checked with the condition holding. *)
component CondExtendChecker
export Executable

trait Ord[\T extends Ord[\T\]\]
  lt(o: T): Boolean
end
trait Add[\T extends Add[\T\]\]
  plus(o: T): T
end
object Num(v: ZZ32) extends { Ord[\Num\], Add[\Num\] }
  lt(o: Num): Boolean = v < o.v
  plus(o: Num): Num = Num(v + o.v)
end
object Str(s: String) extends Ord[\Str\]
  lt(o: Str): Boolean = false
end
object Lst[\E\](a: E, b: E) extends { Ord[\Lst[\E\]\] where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }
  lt(o: Lst[\E\]): Boolean = a.lt(o.a)
end
object Vec[\E\](x: E) extends { Add[\Vec[\E\]\] where { E extends Add[\E\] } }
  plus(o: Vec[\E\]): Vec[\E\] = Vec[\E\](x.plus(o.x))
end

less[\T extends Ord[\T\]\](x: T, y: T): Boolean = x.lt(y)
sum[\T extends Add[\T\]\](x: T, y: T): T = x.plus(y)

146	//         if (ss.size > 0 && ss.exists(!_.isInstanceOf[ArrowType])) pTrue()
147	//         else pSub(NF.makeArrowType(NU.getSpan(x),
148	// 				   NF.makeIntersectionType(toJavaSet(ss.map(_.asInstanceOf[ArrowType].getDomain))),

152	//           pOr(Pairs.distinctPairsFrom(ss).map(tt => pExc(tt._1, tt._2)))) // The second constraint is the only time exclusion is called during subtype checking
153	      pOr(pOr(ss.map(pSub(_, t))),
154	          pOr(Pairs.distinctPairsFrom(ss).map(tt => pExc(tt._1, tt._2)))) // The second constraint is the only time exclusion is called during subtype checking
155	    }
156	    // Union types
157	    case (SUnionType(_,ss), t) =>
158	      pAnd(ss.map(pSub(_, t)))
159	    case (s: TraitType, t@SUnionType(_, ts)) =>
160	      val unionResult = pOr(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))
161	      comprisedTypes(s) match {
162	        case Some(cs) => pOr(unionResult, pAnd(cs.map(pSub(_, t)))) 
163	        case None => unionResult
164	      }
165	    // An inference variable below a union is bounded by the union as a whole: split,
166	    // a solution that holds only of the whole union, as a type variable bounded by
167	    // it, is lost, and the solver meets a disjunction it cannot unify.
168	    case (s: _InferenceVarType, t: UnionType) if !negate => pUpperBound(s, t)
169	    // A type variable is below a union where its bound is, as well as where it is
170	    // below one of the union's members.
171	    case (s@SVarType(_, id, _), t@SUnionType(_, ts)) if !negate =>
172	      val split = pOr(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))
173	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
174	      traits.readContext()
175	      if (history.contains(hEntry)) split
176	      else {
177	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
178	        val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(staticParam(id).getExtendsClause)))(nHistory)
179	        pOr(split, pSub(supers, t)(negate, nHistory))
180	      }
181	    case (s, SUnionType(_, ts)) =>
182	      pOr(ts.map(pSub(s, _)))
183	    // We must eliminate trait self types before making constraints  
184	    case (s: TraitSelfType, t) => pSub(removeSelf(s), t)
185	    case (s, STraitSelfType(_, named, _)) => pSub(s,named)
186	    // Inference variables
187	    case (s: _InferenceVarType, t: _InferenceVarType) =>
188	      pAnd(pUpperBound(s, t), pLowerBound(t,s))
189	    case (s: _InferenceVarType, t) => pUpperBound(s,t)
190	    case (s, t: _InferenceVarType) => pLowerBound(t,s)
191	    /* Type variables are special for several reasons
192	     *  1) Getting the bound out of a type variable is the only place where a type can increase in size during type checking.
193	     *     We use the history to ensure termination.
194	     *  2) They are the only place where you cannot negate using de Morgan's. There is a good explanation of why in the OOPSLA paper.
195	     */
196	    case (s@SVarType(_, sid, _), t@SVarType(_, tid, _)) if (sid == tid 
197	        // || sid.asInstanceOf[Id].getText == tid.asInstanceOf[Id].getText
198	        ) => True
199	            
200	    case (s@SVarType(_, id, _), t) =>
201	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
202	      traits.readContext()
203	      if (history.contains(hEntry)) {
204	        False
205	      } else {
206	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
207	        val sParam = staticParam(id)
208	
209	        def stdResult () =  {
210	          if (negate) {        
211	//	               println("pSubInner 0: FALSE")
212			       pFalse()(!negate)
213			     } else {
214			       // Using pNorm causes the current history to be passed down
215			       val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(sParam.getExtendsClause)))(nHistory)
216	//	               println("pSubInner 1: supers = " + supers)
217			       pSub(supers, t)(negate, nHistory)
218	                     }
219	        }
220	        
221	        val result = 
222	          if (t.isInstanceOf[VarType]) {
223	        	  val v = t.asInstanceOf[VarType].getName()
224	              val lowerParam = staticParam(v)
225	              if (!lowerParam.getDominatesClause().isEmpty()) { 
226	                val lowers = pNorm(makeUnionType(toListFromImmutable(lowerParam.getDominatesClause)))(nHistory)
227	                pSub(s,lowers)
228	              } else {stdResult()}
229	        } else {stdResult()} 
230	        
231	        
232	//	ErrorMsgMaker.printHashCodes = true
233	//	println("...and the result of the recursive pSub is " + result)
234	//	ErrorMsgMaker.printHashCodes = false
235	        result
236	      }
237	    case (s, t@SVarType(_, id, _)) =>
238	      val hEntry = (negate, true, s, t)
239	      traits.readContext()
240	      if (history.contains(hEntry))
241	        False
242	      else {
243	        val nHistory = history + hEntry
244	        val sParam = staticParam(id)
245	        val result = if (negate) {
246			       // Using pNorm causes the current history to be passed down
247			       val supers = pNorm(makeIntersectionType(toListFromImmutable(sParam.getExtendsClause)))(nHistory)
248	//	               println("pSubInner 2: supers = " + supers)
249			       pSub(s, supers)(negate, nHistory)
250			     } else {
251	//	               println("pSubInner 3: BOTTOM")
252			       pSub(s, BOTTOM)
253	                     }
254	//            ErrorMsgMaker.printHashCodes = true
255	//            println("...and the result of the recursive pSub is " + result)
256	//            ErrorMsgMaker.printHashCodes = false
257	        result
258	      }
259	    // Trait types
260	    case (s: TraitType, t: TraitType) if (t==OBJECT) => pTrue()
261	    
262	    case (STraitType(_,traitId_1,staticArgs_1,_),STraitType(_,traitId_2,staticArgs_2,_)) 
263	    	if (typeCons(traitId_1)==typeCons(traitId_2)) =>
264	
265	     // First, let's find the static parameters for trait traitId_1
266		  
267	     val idx = traits.declaredTypeCons(traitId_1.getText())
268	     val staticParams = scalaify(idx.unwrap().staticParameters()).asInstanceOf[List[StaticParam]]
269

840	  }
841	  
842	  // Accessor methods for trait table
843	  def typeCons(x: Id): TypeConsIndex =
844	//    toOption(traits.typeCons(x)).getOrElse(bug(x, x + " is not in the trait table"))
845	    toOption(traits.typeCons(x)).getOrElse(throw new RuntimeException("Not in the trait table: " + x.toStringReadable + " @ " + x.at))
846	
847	  def comprisesClause(t: TraitType): Set[TraitType] = typeCons(t.getName) match {
848	    case ti: ProperTraitIndex =>
849	      val args = toListFromImmutable(t.getArgs)
850	      val params = toListFromImmutable(ti.staticParameters)
851	      toSet(ti.comprisesTypes).map(nt => if (!nt.isInstanceOf[TraitType]) return Set()
852	                                         else openWhereSizes(ti, substitute(args, params, nt), args, params).asInstanceOf[TraitType])
853	    case _ => Set()
854	  }

856	  /* The nat, int and type where-clause variables of a trait declaration with a
857	   * comprises clause, as static parameters: comprises { N[\n\] } where
858	   * [\nat n\] lists N at every n, and comprises { List[\E\] } where [\E\]
859	   * lists List at every E. */
860	  def whereSizes(ti: ProperTraitIndex): List[StaticParam] =
861	    if (ti.comprisesTypes.isEmpty) Nil
862	    else ti.ast match {
863	      case d: TraitObjectDecl => toOption(NU.getWhereClause(d)) match {
864	        case Some(w) => toListFromImmutable(w.getBindings).filter(b =>
865	            b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindNat] || b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindInt] ||
866	            b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindType]).map(b =>
867	            if (b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindType])
868	              NF.makeTypeParam(NU.getSpan(b), b.getName, b.getSupers, none[Type], false)
869	            else
870	            NF.makeStaticParam(NU.getSpan(b), null, b.getName,
871	                               _root_.java.util.Collections.emptyList[BaseType],
872	                               _root_.java.util.Collections.emptyList[BaseType],
873	                               none[Type], false, b.getKind))
874	        case None => Nil
875	      }
876	      case _ => Nil
877	    }
878	
879	  /* Whether t is a trait whose comprises clause lists types at where-clause variables. */
880	  def opensSizes(t: Type): Boolean = t match {
881	    case tt: TraitType => toOption(traits.typeCons(tt.getName)) match {
882	      case Some(ti: ProperTraitIndex) => !whereSizes(ti).isEmpty
883	      case _ => false
884	    }
885	    case _ => false
886	  }

888	  /* Whether t is a trait whose comprises clause lists types at a type where-clause variable. */
889	  def opensTypes(t: Type): Boolean = t match {
890	    case tt: TraitType => toOption(traits.typeCons(tt.getName)) match {
891	      case Some(ti: ProperTraitIndex) => whereSizes(ti).exists(_.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindType])
892	      case _ => false
893	    }
894	    case _ => false
895	  }

897	  /* A type ti's comprises clause lists, each where-clause variable opened: a
898	   * fresh name, equal only to itself (Formula.openedSizeName); a type is
899	   * bounded as its where-clause binding is, at the trait's static arguments
900	   * args for its static parameters params. */
901	  def openWhereSizes(ti: ProperTraitIndex, listed: Type, args: List[StaticArg], params: List[StaticParam]): Type =
902	    whereSizes(ti) match {
903	    case Nil => listed
904	    case ws =>
905	      val opened: List[StaticArg] = ws.map(p =>
906	        if (p.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindType]) {
907	          val id = NF.makeId(NU.getSpan(p), openedSizeName(p.getName.getText))
908	          val bounds = toListFromImmutable(p.getExtendsClause).map(b =>
909	            (if (args.isEmpty) b else substitute(args, params, b)).asInstanceOf[BaseType])
910	          KindEnv.registerOpened(id, NF.makeTypeParam(NU.getSpan(p), id, toJavaList(bounds), none[Type], false))
911	          NF.makeTypeArg(NU.getSpan(p), NF.makeVarType(NU.getSpan(p), id)): StaticArg
912	        } else
913	          NF.makeIntArg(NU.getSpan(p),
914	            NF.makeIntRef(NU.getSpan(p), NF.makeId(NU.getSpan(p), openedSizeName(p.getName.getText)))): StaticArg)
915	      substitute(opened, ws, listed)
916	  }
917	  
918	  // For the purposes of this method Any is not the Parent of Object as it is not a TraitType
919	  def parents(t: TraitType): Set[BaseType] = traits.memoParents(t) {
920	    val STraitType(_, n, a, _) = t
921	    val index = typeCons(n).asInstanceOf[TraitIndex]
922	    toListFromImmutable(index.extendsTypes).
923	      map(tw => substitute(a, toListFromImmutable(index.staticParameters), tw.getBaseType).asInstanceOf[BaseType]).toSet
924	  }

928	      case s:TraitType => Set(s) ++ ancestors(s)
929	      case x => Set(x)

932	  def comprisedTypes(t: TraitType): Option[Set[BaseType]] = {
933	    val STraitType(_, n, a, _) = t
934	    typeCons(n) match {
935	      case index: ProperTraitIndex =>
936		val cs = index.comprisesTypes
937		if (cs.isEmpty) None
938	        else
939		    Some(toSet(cs).map(typ => openWhereSizes(index, substitute(a, toListFromImmutable(index.staticParameters), typ),
940		                                             a, toListFromImmutable(index.staticParameters)).asInstanceOf[BaseType]).toSet)
941	      case _ => None
942	    }
943	  }

945	  /* The analyzer in which a type an excludes clause names is read: a trait that excludes
946	   * another is added to the other's clause at its own static parameters
947	   * (IndexBuilder.checkTraitClauses), which are not in scope where that clause is read,
948	   * so the ones not in scope are added. */
949	  private def withClauseParams(e: TraitType): TypeAnalyzer = {
950	    val free = toListFromImmutable(e.getArgs).collect {
951	      case STypeArg(_, _, SVarType(_, n, _)) if { traits.readContext(); !env.contains(n) } => n.getText }
952	    if (free.isEmpty) this
953	    else typeCons(e.getName) match {
954	      case ti: TraitIndex =>
955	        val params = toListFromImmutable(ti.staticParameters).filter(p => free.contains(p.getName.getText))
956	        if (params.isEmpty) this else extend(params, None)
957	      case _ => this
958	    }
959	  }
960	
961	  def excludesClause(t: TraitType): Set[TraitType] = traits.memoExcludesClause(t) {
962	    val ti = typeCons(t.getName).asInstanceOf[TraitIndex]
963	    val args = toListFromImmutable(t.getArgs)
964	    val params = toListFromImmutable(ti.staticParameters)
965	    val excludes = ti match{
966	      case ti : ProperTraitIndex =>
967	        toSet(ti.excludesTypes).map(substitute(args, params, _).asInstanceOf[TraitType])
968	      case _ => Set[TraitType]()
969	    }
970	    val supers = toListFromImmutable(ti.extendsTypes).map(tw => substitute(args, params, tw.getBaseType))
971	    val transitively = supers.flatMap{
972	      case s: TraitType => excludesClause(s)
973	      case _ => Set[TraitType]()
974	    }
975	    excludes ++ transitively
976	  }

22	/**
23	 * Represents a list of variable name to static parameter bindings for some
24	 * context. All instances of this class should be created with `KindEnv.makeFresh`
25	 * or with the `extend` method.
26	 */
27	abstract sealed class KindEnv extends StaticEnv[StaticParam] {
28	
29	  /** My type. */
30	  type Env = KindEnv
31	
32	  /** My binding type. */
33	  type EnvBinding = KindBinding
34	
35	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given node. */
36	  def extend(node: Node): KindEnv =
37	    new NestedKindEnv(this, KindEnv.extractNodeBindings(node))
38	
39	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given nodes. */
40	  def extend[T <: Node](nodes: Iterable[T]): KindEnv =
41	    new NestedKindEnv(this, nodes.flatMap(KindEnv.extractNodeBindings))
42	
43	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given node. */
44	  def extend(node: Node, where: Option[WhereClause]): KindEnv = {
45	    val whereBindings = where.map(KindEnv.extractNodeBindings)
46	                             .getOrElse(Iterable.empty)
47	    val nodeBindings = KindEnv.extractNodeBindings(node)
48	    val declared = whereBindings ++ nodeBindings
49	    new NestedKindEnv(this, declared ++ KindEnv.constraintBounds(this, declared, where))
50	  }
51	
52	  /** Extend me with the immediate bindings of the given nodes. */
53	  def extend[T<:Node](nodes: Iterable[T], where: Option[WhereClause]): KindEnv = {
54	    val whereBindings = where.map(KindEnv.extractNodeBindings)
55	                             .getOrElse(Iterable.empty)
56	    val nodesBindings = nodes.flatMap(KindEnv.extractNodeBindings)
57	    val declared = whereBindings ++ nodesBindings
58	    new NestedKindEnv(this, declared ++ KindEnv.constraintBounds(this, declared, where))
59	  }
60	
61	  /**
62	   * Get the type of the given variable name, if it is bound. The resulting
63	   * type will only be defined if this name maps to a bool, int, or nat static
64	   * parameter.
65	   */
66	  def getType(x: Name): Option[Type] = lookup(x).flatMap(b =>
67	    b.sparam.getKind match {
68	      case _:KindBool => Some(Types.BOOLEAN)
69	      case _:KindInt => Some(Types.INT_LITERAL)
70	      case _:KindNat => Some(Types.INT_LITERAL)
71	      case _ => None
72	    })
73	
74	  def staticParam(x: Name): Option[StaticParam] = lookup(x).map(_.sparam)
75	}
76	
77	/** The single empty kind environment. */
78	protected object EmptyKindEnv extends KindEnv with EmptyStaticEnv[StaticParam] {
79	  // A type opened from a value is found in every environment, as a size
80	  // opened from a value needs no binding.
81	  override def lookup(x: Name): Option[KindBinding] = KindEnv.lookupOpened(x)
82	}
83	
84	/**
85	 * A kind environment with a parent and some explicit bindings.
86	 *
87	 * @param parent A kind environment that this one extends.
88	 * @param _bindings A collection of all the bindings in this environment.
89	 */
90	class NestedKindEnv (protected val parent: KindEnv,
91	                               _bindings: Iterable[KindBinding])
92	    extends KindEnv with NestedStaticEnv[StaticParam] {
93	
94	  /** Internal representation of `bindings` is a map. */
95	  val bindings: Map[Name, KindBinding] =
96	    Map(_bindings.map(b => (b.name, b)).toSeq:_*)
97	}
98	
99	/** Companion module for KindEnv; contains "static" members. */
100	object KindEnv extends StaticEnvCompanion[StaticParam] {
101	
102	  /** My type. */
103	  type Env = KindEnv
104	
105	  /** My binding type. */
106	  type EnvBinding = KindBinding
107	
108	  /** Creates a fresh kind environment. */
109	  def makeFresh: KindEnv = EmptyKindEnv.extend(Nil)
110	
111	  /**
112	   * The bindings that the where clause's trait constraints give: each type
113	   * variable X named by a constraint X extends B, bound in the declared
114	   * bindings or outside them, rebound with B added to its bounds.
115	   */
116	  def constraintBounds(outer: KindEnv, declared: Iterable[KindBinding],
117	                       where: Option[WhereClause]): Iterable[KindBinding] = where match {
118	    case Some(SWhereClause(_, _, constraints)) =>
119	      val scope = new NestedKindEnv(outer, declared)
120	      val byName = constraints.collect { case SWhereExtends(_, name, supers) => (name, supers) }
121	      val names = byName.map(_._1).foldLeft(List[Id]())((acc, n) =>
122	        if (acc.exists(_.getText == n.getText)) acc else acc :+ n)
123	      names.flatMap(n => scope.lookup(n) match {
124	        case Some(KindBinding(bn, sp)) if sp.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindType] =>
125	          val extra = byName.filter(_._1.getText == n.getText).flatMap(_._2)
126	          val supers = toListFromImmutable(sp.getExtendsClause) ++ extra
127	          List(KindBinding(bn, NF.makeStaticParam(sp, sp.getName.asInstanceOf[Id], toJavaList(supers))))
128	        case _ => Nil
129	      })
130	    case _ => Nil
131	  }
132	
133	  /** Extract out the bindings in node. */
134	  protected def extractNodeBindings(node: Node) : Iterable[KindBinding] =
135	    node match {
136	      // Trivially add this param.
137	      case p:StaticParam => Iterable(KindBinding(p.getName, p))
138	      
139	      // Extract bindings from generic declaration.
140	      case g:Generic =>
141	        toListFromImmutable(g.getHeader.getStaticParams)
142	          .map(p => KindBinding(p.getName, p))
143	      
144	      // Extract where clause bindings.
145	      case SWhereClause(info, bindings, _) => bindings.map {
146	        
147	        // If a type binding, create a new TypeParam.
148	        case b:WhereBinding if b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindType] =>
149	          val sp = NF.makeTypeParam(info.getSpan, b.getName, b.getSupers, none[Type], false)
150	          KindBinding(b.getName, sp)
151	
152	        // A nat or int binding is a size, as a nat or int static parameter is.
153	        case b:WhereBinding if b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindNat] || b.getKind.isInstanceOf[KindInt] =>
154	          val sp = NF.makeStaticParam(info.getSpan, null, b.getName,
155	                                      java.util.Collections.emptyList[BaseType],
156	                                      java.util.Collections.emptyList[BaseType],
157	                                      none[Type], false, b.getKind)
158	          KindBinding(b.getName, sp)
159	
160	        // Other kinds not supported yet.
161	        case _ => NI.nyi("non-type where clause bindings")
162	      }
163	
164	      case _ => Iterable.empty
165	    }
166	
167	  /* The types opened from values (TypeAnalyzer.openWhereSizes), each a fresh
168	   * name (Formula.openedSizeName) bound as its where-clause binding bounds it
169	   * at the trait's static arguments. A name is registered once and never
170	   * rebound, so an answer that reads its bound depends on the name alone. */
171	  private val opened = new java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap[String, KindBinding]()
172	
173	  def registerOpened(id: Id, sp: StaticParam): Unit = opened.put(id.getText, KindBinding(id, sp))
174	
175	  def lookupOpened(x: Name): Option[KindBinding] = x match {
176	    case i: Id if i.getApiName.isNone && i.getText.contains("#") => Option(opened.get(i.getText))
177	    case _ => None
178	  }
179	}

182	 * A binding for a kind environment contains name to static parameter pairs.
183	 *
184	 * @param name The variable name for the binding.
185	 * @param sparam The static parameter that this name is binding.
186	 */
187	case class KindBinding(name: Name,
188	                       sparam: StaticParam)

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,

component OverrideConditionalExtensionWalk
export Executable

(* A generic trait that extends a trait under a where clause bounding its static parameter by ZZ32 overrides, with an override over ZZ32, the declaration it inherits there over that parameter, so the program loads and runs it, under walk (traits.tex, sections "Traits" and "Method Declarations"). *)

trait A[\T\]
  f(x: T): String = "A"
end
trait G[\T\] extends A[\T\] where { T extends ZZ32 }
  override f(x: ZZ32): String = "G"
end
object O extends G[\ZZ32\] end

run(): () = do
    assert(O.f(3), "G", "G's f over ZZ32 overrides A[\\T\\]'s over T, which G extends where T extends ZZ32 (traits.tex, section \"Method Declarations\")")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

component conditionalExtension

export Executable

trait PartialOrderAndBoundedLattice[\T, opr LEOPR, opr MINOPR, opr MAXOPR\] end
trait Identity[\opr PLUS\] end

trait RationalQuantity[\unit U absorbs unit, bool ninf, bool lt, bool eq,
                        bool gt, bool pinf, bool nan\]
    extends {
      RationalQuantity[\U, ninf', lt', eq', gt', pinf', nan'\]
              where [\bool ninf', bool lt', bool eq', bool gt', bool pinf',
                      bool nan' \]
                    { ninf IMPLIES ninf', lt IMPLIES lt',
                      eq IMPLIES eq', gt IMPLIES gt', pinf IMPLIES pinf',
                      nan IMPLIES nan'
                    },
              PartialOrderAndBoundedLattice[\RationalQuantity[\U, ninf, lt, eq, gt, pinf, nan\], <=, MIN, MAX\]
              where { ninf AND pinf AND NOT nan }
            }
    where { ninf OR lt OR eq OR gt OR pinf OR nan }
  coerce(x: Identity[\+\]) = 0
end

run() = println "Conditional extension with where clauses can be parsed."

end

component XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk
export Executable

(* A generic object that extends a trait under a where clause on its static parameter is that trait only at the instances where the clause holds, so a type test of an instance whose static argument fails the clause answers false, under walk (trait-parameters.tex, section "Where Clauses"). *)

trait Shows
  show(): String
end
object Word(s: String) extends Shows
  show(): String = s
end
object Box[\E\](x: E) extends { Shows where { E extends Shows } }
  show(): String = x.show()
end

shows(v: Any): Boolean = typecase v of
    Shows => true
    else => false
  end

run(): () = do
    assert(shows(Box[\Word\](Word("w"))), true, "a box of words shows, since Word extends Shows")
    assert(shows(Box[\ZZ32\](1)), false, "a box of integers does not show, since ZZ32 does not extend Shows")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

object Box[\E\](x: E) extends { Shows where { E extends Shows } }
  show(): String = x.show()
end

shows(v: Any): Boolean = typecase v of
    Shows => true
    else => false
  end

    assert(shows(Box[\ZZ32\](1)), false, "a box of integers does not show, since ZZ32 does not extend Shows")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

trait List[\E\] extends { AnyList, LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] }
        excludes { Number, HasRank, String }
  (** %left% and %extractLeft% return the leftmost element in the list
      (and in the latter case, the remainder of the list without its
      leftmost element).  They return %Nothing% if the list is empty.
      %right% and %extractRight% do the same with the rightmost
      element. *)
  getter left():Maybe[\E\]
  getter right():Maybe[\E\]
  abstract getter extractLeft(): Maybe[\(E,List[\E\])\]
  abstract getter extractRight(): Maybe[\(List[\E\],E)\]
  getter reverse(): List[\E\]
  (** the operator %||% returns a list containing the elements of %self% followed
      by the elements of %f% *)
  abstract opr ||(self, other:List[\E\]): List[\E\]
  (** %addLeft% and %addRight% add an element to the left or right of
      the list, respectively *)
  abstract addLeft(e:E):List[\E\]
  abstract addRight(e:E):List[\E\]
  (** %take% returns the leftmost %n% elements of the list; if the
      list is shorter than this, the entire list is returned. *)
  abstract take(n:ZZ32): List[\E\]
  (** %drop% drops the leftmost %n% elements of the list; if the list
      is shorter than this, an empty list is returned. *)
  abstract drop(n:ZZ32): List[\E\]
  abstract opr [n:ZZ32]: E
  (** %l.split(n)% is equivalent to %(l.take(n),l.drop(n))%.  Note in
      particular that appending its results yields the original
      list. *)
  abstract split(n:ZZ32): (List[\E\], List[\E\])
  (** %split% splits the list into two smaller lists.  If %|l| > 1%
      both lists will be non-empty. *)
  abstract split(): (List[\E\], List[\E\])
  filter(p: E -> Boolean): List[\E\]
  (** %concatMap% is an in-place version of the %nest% method from
      %Generator%; it flattens the result into an actual list, rather than
      returning an abstract %Generator%. *)
  concatMap[\G\](f: E->List[\G\]): List[\G\]
end

(** Vararg factory for lists; provides aggregate list constants: *)
opr <|[\E\] xs: E... |>: List[\E\]
(** List comprehensions: *)
opr BIG <|[\T\]|>:Comprehension[\T,List[\T\],List[\T\],List[\T\]\]
opr BIG <|[\T\] g:Generator[\T\]|>:List[\T\]

opr BIG CONCAT[\T\](): BigReduction[\List[\T\],List[\T\]\]
opr BIG CONCAT[\T\](g: Generator[\List[\T\]\]):List[\T\]

(** Convert generator into list (simpler type than comprehension above): *)
list[\E\](g:Generator[\E\]):List[\E\]

(** Flatten a list of lists *)
concat[\E\](lists:Indexed[\List[\E\],ZZ32\]):List[\E\]

emptyList[\E\](): List[\E\]

(** %emptyList[\E\](n)% allocates an empty list that can accept %n%
    %addRight% operations without reallocating the underlying storage. **)
emptyList[\E\](n:ZZ32): List[\E\]

singleton[\E\](e:E): List[\E\]

(** A reduction object for concatenating lists. *)
object Concat[\E\] extends MonoidReduction[\ List[\E\] \]
  empty(): List[\E\]
  join(a:List[\E\], b:List[\E\]): List[\E\]
end

transpose[\E,F\](xs: List[\(E,F)\]): (List[\E\], List[\F\])

end

A trait or object that extends a type under a where clause of trait
constraints only is that type exactly where the constraints hold: parents
leaves such an entry out, conditionalParents gives it with its conditions
at the type's static arguments, and the subtype case of a trait type counts
it where they hold, as a formula (beside rung A's reading of a parent that
opens, which it keeps). KindEnv.withExtendsConditions adds the conditions to
the declaration's where clause, so that its members and its extends clause
are checked with them holding (Decls' and TypeWellFormedChecker's trait and
object cases). From the where-clause probe's B.3, re-based onto climb batch
17.

The library: LexicographicOrder's element bounded by StandardTotalOrder;
List (and PureList's List) extends LexicographicOrder under that condition,
with ZeroIndexed written outside it; a structural = kept on List with
LexicographicOrder's body, so that a list of unordered elements keeps its
equality; the team's comment 'a hack to avoid the error of overloaded
methods' removed above the generic distribute it no longer describes.

Edits the original tree: TypeAnalyzer.scala, KindEnv.scala, Decls.scala,
TypeWellFormedChecker.scala, FortressLibrary.fsi/.fss, List.fsi/.fss,

facts-extract: part 1 of 1. Its 1 part prints 2393 bytes, about 1100 tokens.
Asked for, and where it is:
  doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2931-2967  [2064 bytes]

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2931-2967

\subsection{The interpreter's choice of a coercion}
\seclabel{revival-coercion-walk}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{resolving-coercion}.
\item[Change] One box after the example of the paragraph that says that
coercion is resolved statically; the paragraph and its example are unchanged.
The box says that the compiled path follows the text; that the interpreter,
which has no static types, chooses a coercion on the value and so runs
\EXP{f(B)} for the example's \EXP{f(c)}, and answers the same way wherever an
argument's value is of a type that another declaration already fits; that both
cases are gated as expected failures; and that the interpreter is to follow the
text once it takes the coercions that the compiled type checker inserts.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the interpreter's choice of a coercion on the value is
its limit, since it has no static types from which to resolve a coercion
statically, and that the interpreter is made to follow the text once the
compiled type checker checks the programs it runs and it takes the coercions the
checker inserts.
The type group's paper of 2019 also carries the static types of calls to run
time for its dispatcher, which the interpreter does not have.
\item[Effect] None on the language.
The interpreter's answer, 4 where the text gives 3, and its answer in the
narrower case are gated by
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss} and
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss} (row~19 of
the revival's gap ledger).
\item[Original text] The passage is unchanged:
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, lines
567--604, which begin:
\begin{quote}
Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is statically
chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted into the call.
This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

facts-extract: end of part 1 of 1, the last.
longer valid. The compiled type checker refuses them where the arguments
that differ are types, or numerals given as \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
arguments (row~402 of the revival's gap ledger). It does not yet refuse
them where those arguments are \KWD{bool} arguments, though it accepts boolean parameters written out (row~406),
or where one of them is a static parameter of the trait or object that extends both (row~414).
The interpreter does not check the rule.
The number chapters are revised to the reorganized numeric types
(\secref{revival-numbers}).
\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 states no such
property; its relations are ``the smallest ones that satisfy all the
properties given in those sections (and this one)''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex}, lines
185--189), and the properties it gives for trait types are these (lines
212--216):
\begin{quote}
A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
in which case the defined trait type
excludes every type that appears in that clause.
Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
\end{quote}
Its rule on declarations is only that of exclusive traits,
``no trait can extend them both''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 218--222).
\item[Route C] Replaces this rule by the rule of \secref{revival-routec}.
\end{description}

\subsection{Where-clause variables in extends clauses}
\seclabel{revival-where}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{where-clauses}; \secref{trait-decls}.
\item[Change] One sentence is added: a \KWD{where}-clause variable may not
appear as a static argument in an \KWD{extends} clause.
The three declarations that followed it are kept, marked
``Not allowed'', each with the way to write it
(\secref{revival-covariance}, \secref{revival-every},
\secref{revival-empty}).
A box after Victor Luchangco's two draft notes in \secref{trait-decls},
which say that a trait can explicitly extend itself through hidden type
variables and that ``we could just rule this a special case'', answers
them.
\item[Rationale] Such a variable makes the declared type a subtype of one
instantiation for each type the variable may stand for, and instantiation
exclusion forbids any two of them.
\item[Effect] None of the three declarations ran before the revision:
both implementations stop at name resolution, because a
\KWD{where}-clause variable is not in scope in an \KWD{extends} clause.
The revision makes that the rule.
The calculus of \appref{where-calculus} still admits such
declarations (\secref{revival-calculi}).
\item[Original text] No such sentence; the draft notes are unchanged.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C, which places no type below
infinitely many instantiations of one trait.
\end{description}

parameters are stated to be invariant, and a widening function with

\subsection{The implicit bound of a type parameter}
\seclabel{revival-bound}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{type-param}; \secref{principles-overloading}.
\item[Change] A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause has the
implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}'' in place of
``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}'', with a box.
The restriction of \chapref{overloaded-declarations} that a functional whose
single parameter's type is a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any} cannot be
overloaded is stated for a bound written \TYP{Any}, and a sentence says that a
type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause does not fall under it,
with \library's value factory of one-dimensional arrays as its example, and a
box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival took
\TYP{Any} as the implicit bound on 27~September 2026 and decided it on
29~September 2026.
\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples, functions and \TYP{()} among them; the
team's later Types chapter makes \TYP{Object} a supertype of every trait type,
arrow type and function type that excludes \TYP{()} and every tuple type
(Luchangco, 2012,
\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
232--236, in the revival's repository).
\Library\ instantiate type parameters declared without a bound at tuple types,
an array indexed by pairs among them, which the bound \TYP{Object} would refuse;
the interpreter, and the compiled type checker when it checks \library, read
such a parameter as bounded by \TYP{Any}.
The type group's paper of 2019 gives the same default: ``By default, each type
parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom'' (Park, Hong, Steele
and Ryu, POPL 2019, Section~3.2).
Under the implicit bound \TYP{Any}, the restriction on a naked type parameter of
bound \TYP{Any} would forbid overloading every functional whose single
parameter's type is a type parameter declared without a bound, \library's
factory \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket(v\COLON{}T)}
beside \EXP{{array}_{1}\llbracket{}T, \KWD{nat}\:s_{0}\rrbracket()} among them;
the compiled type checker applies the restriction only to a bound written
\TYP{Any}, and draws no such refusal on \library.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] A type parameter declared without a bound may be instantiated
with a tuple type or with \TYP{()}.
The compiled path still gives such a type parameter of a program's own
declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a
divergence that lasts until the compiled path is switched over to the
interpreter's library.
The rationale of \secref{revival-tabulate}, written before this change, speaks
of the implicit bound \TYP{Object}.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex},
lines 49--50:
\begin{quote}
If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}'' clause.
\end{quote}
and \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines
114--116:
\begin{quote}
In addition, a functional which takes a single parameter of type a naked type
parameter of bound \TYP{Any} cannot be overloaded.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

## 11. Decisions, findings, questions

**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers 1 to 6.

1. **The split in order (variant B).** Rejected:
   - variant C, which tests `Node` first and skips 213 tests for leaves: 332 s against B's 344 s, one run
     each, within noise; its exactness needs a proof (every node class implements `Node`);
   - the JVM switch alone: 652 s, and a switch every JVM would need;
   - a class-keyed dispatch.
2. **30 cases per method.** The largest method is 4,474 bytes, against the limit of 8,000.
3. **The patch changes the generator and the file it writes, not the file alone.** A build would otherwise
   regenerate the old walker the next time `Fortress.ast` or a generator changes.
4. **An audit by branch index, not by memo hits.** The fix adds no memo.
5. **The test is in Java**, because of the scalac 2.13 limit (§8).
6. **The brief's "distance stage is `tools/count-run/`" read as `tools/distance/run.sh`.** `count-run.sh`
   runs each interpreter test under walk.

**Findings.**
- The interpreted walker (§2.2).
- The shares of the repair (+267 s) and of rung C (+109 s before the fix, +65 s after) (§3).
- After the fix, about 95 % of the component's time is in the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3).
- The checker's output depends on identity hashes (§9).
- The repair removes the distance stage's crash row and adds no site (§6).
- The other methods over the limit are negligible after the fix (§2.2).

**Defects.**
- **The interpreted walker.** My change repairs it (way 1), pinned by `WalkerJUTest`. No ledger row holds it;
  the row to write:
  - claim: the generated `Walker.walk` (`FortressAst.scala`, from `ScalaAstGenerator.java`) is 31,704 bytes
    of bytecode, past HotSpot's 8,000-byte huge-method limit, so the JVM never compiles it, and every phase
    that walks a tree runs it in the interpreter;
  - status: NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, closed by the fix's commit;
  - class: implementation gap (generator, speed);
  - spec: silent;
  - reproducer: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`;
  - found by: this probe.
- **The identity-hash dependence.** A note for row 488, with the H runs' commands and outputs (§9).

**Sentences of the specification made false:** none.

**For FACTS.**
1. **The fact.** The generated AST walker's `walk` was one method over HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit, so it ran
   interpreted. With it split in order, the count stage with row 680's repair takes 352 s instead of 911 s,
   and the distance stage 931 s instead of 2,375 s, with identical output.
   - What it means: row 680's line can land under the 690 s rule.
   - Test: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`.
   - Detail: §2.2 and §6.
2. **The fact.** The checker's output depends on the JVM's identity-hash sequence, because AST hashes include
   the `Class` identity hash. One extra identity hash at start reorders the api checks and the members of
   unions in messages.
   - What it means: the stages' outputs can move with an unrelated edit (row 488).
   - Command: the driver with `-Dprobe.hashes=1`.
   - Detail: §9.
3. **The fact.** Rung C's normal form costs 12 % of the count stage before the fix, 19 % after.
   - Detail: §3.

**Questions for the curator (decisions not taken).**
- Q1: land the walker split as its own rung ahead of row 680's line, or in the same rung?
- Q2: pursue the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3), about 95 % of what remains?
  - Ways: a memo of normalized meets shared across analyzers; fewer reductions in `Formula.and`'s fold.
- Q3: make AST hashing independent of identity hashes (row 488)? That would change iteration orders, and so
  message text, once.

**Commands worked out.**
- **JFR, read without the text dump.** A single-file Java program over `jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile`
  aggregates `jdk.ExecutionSample` within an epoch window, by self, inclusive, callers or callees. A frame's
  `getType()` (Interpreted, JIT compiled, Inlined) shows which methods the JVM never compiled.
- **Methods over the limit:** a `java.lang.classfile` scan of `ProjectFortress/build` for `Code` attributes
  longer than 8,000 bytes.
- **The AST generators by hand, in scratch:**
  1. `javac -cp <scala jars>:ProjectFortress/build:ProjectFortress/third_party/astgen/astgen.jar -d <dir>/build ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/*.java`.
  2. Copy `Fortress.ast` into `<dir>/astgen`.
  3. From there, `java -cp <dir>/build:<scala jars>:ProjectFortress/build:astgen.jar edu.rice.cs.astgen.ASTGen Fortress.ast`. The `.ast` file's `customClassPath ../build` finds the generators.
- **A huge method's compile attempts:** `-XX:-DontCompileHugeMethods -XX:+PrintCompilation`.
- **Moving the identity-hash sequence:** a driver copy that calls `new Object().hashCode()` N times before
  the phases.

## 10. Decisions, findings, questions

**Decisions.**

1. I shared only answers whose computation read no context. This chooses exactness over reach. The alternatives:
   - TypeScript's rule, dualized: a true answer found under the history's cuts is true without them. It shares
     more, but it can change nested answers, and with them the per-analyzer normal forms.
   - Keys renamed apart, plus the variables' bounds, shared across analyzers.
   - Fuel or depth limits, which change answers.
   - Library-side changes: drop `IntLiteral` from `Number`'s clause, or keep `T extends Number`. These change the
     library, not the checker.
2. Only `True` and `False` are shared, not constraint formulas.
3. A hit in the analyzer's own memo counts as a context read. This is conservative.
4. The memo lives on `TraitTable`, behind its own switch, following rung M.
5. The refusal test carries the `XXX` prefix, by the team's convention.

No decision of the curator covers 1 to 5.

**Findings for the record.**

- The slowdown is recomputation, with the numbers of §2 and §3.
- The count stage on this tree takes about 300 s for the base, measured once at load 0.31. That is not "seconds",
  and the base's `checkApi FortressLibrary` takes 74 s under the fix.
- The overloading stage's error order is not fixed between runs (by reading, §7).
- Noticed by reading, not verified: `withClauseParams` decides by name whether a type variable in an excludes
  clause is in scope (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:820`). So an analyzer whose own parameter has the same name as the
  clause's could read the clause through its own bound. The fix counts that test as a context read.

**Questions for the curator (decisions not taken).**

- Q1: carry the fix as a rung ahead of fork 2's library half, or with it, or hold both until the distance stage's
  remaining gap (1,032 s against 819 s at the landed gate, not a pair) is also closed?
- Q2: pursue the further exact steps of §9?

**Commands worked out.**

- **Compile the fix into a shadow folder.** Two Scala files at once:
  `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d <dir> -encoding UTF-8 TraitTable.scala TypeAnalyzer.scala`.
  Then prefix `<dir>` to the classpath in copies of the stage scripts.
- **Run compiled `.test` files through the harness on shadow classes:**
  `FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "<dir>:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit <absolute .test paths>`.
- **JFR with deep stacks:**
  `-XX:FlightRecorderOptions:stackdepth=2048 -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=...,settings=profile,dumponexit=true`.
  `jcmd <JVM pid> JFR.dump name=1 filename=...` takes a copy mid-run, and
  `jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample --stack-depth 2048` reads it.
  - The default 250 MB cap keeps only the last few minutes.
  - Aim `jstack` and `jcmd` at the `java` process, never at the stage's `timeout` wrapper. A dump aimed at the
    wrapper killed a run.

# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath
javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$SCRATCH/classes" \
      "$D/WorldFlip.java" "$D/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
      > "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" 2>&1
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then
    echo "checker-count: javac failed; see $SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; tail -20 "$SCRATCH/javac.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 2. run the compiler phase order over the interpreter's library under a private cache
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 10 900 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches="$SCRATCH/caches" \
       -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=$OVERLOAD_CACHE \
       -cp "$SCRATCH/classes:$CP" WorldFlip "$TARGET" ) > "$SCRATCH/run.txt" 2>&1
RC=$?
if ! grep -q 'has [0-9]* errors\?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" ; then
    echo "checker-count: the run printed no error total (rc=$RC); see $SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2
    tail -20 "$SCRATCH/run.txt" >&2 ; exit 1
fi

# 3. the table. One row per api the checker named, its own error count as the
#    instrumented checker printed it; then the total, the number of distinct
#    file:line the errors were reported at, and the first crash the checker
#    survived. Rows are sorted so that two runs of the same tree are byte-equal.
{
    printf '#api\terrors\n'
    grep '^@@PROBE checkApi .* -> errors=' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" \
        | sed -E 's/^@@PROBE checkApi ([^ ]+) -> errors=([0-9]+)$/\1\t\2/' | sort -u
    printf '#total\t%s\n' "$(grep -oE 'has [0-9]+ errors?\.$' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | tail -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+')"
    printf '#locations\t%s\n' "$(grep -oE '^/[^ ]+:[0-9]+:' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | sort -u | wc -l | tr -d ' ')"
    crash=$(grep -m1 '^@@PROBE OverloadingChecker CRASHED on ' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" | sed 's/^@@PROBE //')
    site=$(grep -m1 -A6 '^@@PROBE OverloadingChecker CRASHED on ' "$SCRATCH/run.txt" \
           | grep -oE '\([A-Za-z0-9_$]+\.(scala|java):[0-9]+\)' | grep -v '(NI\.java:' \
           | head -1 | tr -d '()')      # the first frame that is not the nyi helper itself
    printf '#crash\t%s\n' "${crash:-none}${site:+ at $site}"
    printf '#cache\toverloading memo %s (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=%s)\n' \
           "$( [ "$OVERLOAD_CACHE" = false ] && echo off || echo on )" "$OVERLOAD_CACHE"
    if [ "$(sha256sum < "$STOCK" | cut -d' ' -f1)" = "$STOCK_SHA" ] ; then
        printf '#shadow\tmatches the tracked StaticChecker\n'
    else
        printf '#shadow\tSTALE: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java has changed since the copy was taken; refresh the copy and the checksum in run.sh\n'
    fi
} > "$OUT"

cat "$OUT"
echo "# checker-count: full output $SCRATCH/run.txt, rc=$RC"

&$|$& \emph{UnitExpr}\\

\end{GrammarTwo}

Syntactically, a trait declaration starts with
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
\KWD{trait}, followed by the name of the trait,
an optional sequence of static parameters (described in
\chapref{trait-parameters}),
an optional set of \emph{extended} traits,
an optional set of \emph{excluded} traits,
an optional set of \emph{comprises} on the trait,
an optional \KWD{where} clause (described in \secref{where-clauses}),
zero or more \emph{coercion} declarations
(discussed in \chapref{conversions-coercions}),
zero or more declarations of abstract fields,
getter and setter methods,
and zero or more declarations of methods
separated by newlines or semicolons,
that are not getters or setters,
and finally \KWD{end}.
A trait declaration may end with an optional \KWD{trait} and its name again.
It is a static error if the identifier after \KWD{end} is not the name of the trait being declared.
Property declarations (described in \secref{property-decls}) can be freely
commingled with the declarations of methods and abstract fields.
An \KWD{extends} clause comes first, if any, and
\KWD{excludes},
\KWD{comprises},
and \KWD{where}
clauses come in any order.

Each of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises} clauses consists
of \KWD{extends}, \KWD{excludes}, and \KWD{comprises}
respectively followed by a set of trait references
separated by commas and enclosed in braces `\txt{\{}' and `\txt{\}}'.
If such a clause contains only one trait, the enclosing braces may be elided.

content.content:
## 2. Your answers this batch takes, and the coordinator's calls it builds

### Two questions for you, one per item, each with its default

1. **Item 60, row 766: which way walk repairs a trait's generic dotted method.** Way A reads the method's bounds and coercion targets in the trait's method environment, where its instances already read their types (`way-a.patch`); every trait value then equals the same method's in an object and as a function, and the compiled values do not move (the probe, section 5). Way D gives every trait method that environment, which reaches the overload comparisons and member lookup, and the team kept the two apart ("not yet, it changes overloading semantics", `GenericMethod.java:91-92`). Way C restores the base's loud refusal, which keeps P-48 by stopping and gives none of the checker's values. **Default: A**, rung W. It reverses nothing: P-46, P-48 and P-74 ask for these values.
2. **A list of floats: ordered or not under conditional extension.** The rung bounds `LexicographicOrder`'s element by `StandardTotalOrder`, as the judgement's bound and the team's advanced library do (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`), so the checker gives no order to a list of `RR64`, `QQ` or `Range` values, which are partially ordered; the text says such a list is "partial or total depending on whether the ordering of the elements is partial or total" (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:519-522`). A second entry under `StandardPartialOrder` would need a lexicographic partial order that the team did not write. Walk keeps today's behaviour for such lists until walk's half lands. **Default: one entry, no order for such a list on the checker**, by P-151's "add nothing it did not", stated in Appendix I's new entry. It can be undone: the other way adds an entry and its trait later.

### The coordinator's calls this batch builds, listed for your review

Each is settled by the record's principles and is reversible; none reverses a decision of yours, so none holds the batch.

1. **Way A's two measured lines kept as the probe left them.** The bound read at `EvaluatorBase.java:491` is kept, since a bound that names another static parameter needs it; `inferByUnification` at `:875` is left, since reading the bound there moved no value and turned one refusal into the function path's internal error (the probe, section 4).
2. **The message names the rule by the specification's name**, as the checker names its own: the No Duplicates Rule keeps walk's message for equal domains, "fails because their parameter lists have the same types"; the Return Type Rule and the Meet Rule each get theirs. Six tests key on the old message, not two: `GenericReturnRuleInvariantWalk` and `GenericReturnRuleOuterParamWalk`, which the review names because they pass on any refusal, and `NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, `NoDuplicatesRuleSizeWalk`, `GenericOverloadInstancesApartWalk` and `GenericBoundsNoMeetWalk`. Each is rekeyed to the rule its own comment names.
3. **Conditional extension split from the four rows**, for its size, and row 753 added to rung K, since row 771's note says it waits on 753.
4. **Members checked under the condition, as P-151 says, and not yet scoped to it.** A member so checked stays callable where the condition fails, the probe's hole. Scoping it needs a dotted call's check of a condition on the trait's parameter, which rung K builds as row 748, so it waits for the batch after; rung X files it as NEW-X-1. The team's own note foresaw it: "With conditional subtyping (or conditional methods), we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular method" (`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex`, its subsection "No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked Type Variables").
5. **Walk's half waits.** Walk reads an extension under a `where` clause as holding at every instance, and checks an override under it since climb batch 13 (`e8d377669`). Rung X files the reading as NEW-X-2 with an expected-failure walk test. Building it would change walk's values: a list of tuples or of floats would lose its `<` under walk.
6. **A structural `=` on `List`, outside the condition**, with `LexicographicOrder`'s body, as the judgement asks: without it a list of pairs, not ordered, falls to the identity `=` on the checker (`NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss:48` compares such lists).
7. **Only an `extends` clause of constraints alone is conditional**; a clause that binds a new variable keeps today's reading (the probe's B.6), and Appendix I's "Where-clause variables in extends clauses" bars such a variable from an `extends` clause.
8. **The team's comment "a hack to avoid the error of overloaded methods"** (`FortressLibrary.fss:3232`), now above the team's real generic `distribute`, is removed by rung X, the next library rung, as PLAN's default for the review's finding 7 says.
9. **Row 749's repair makes the checker refuse a call that the team's walk test runs**: `GenericFnWithExcludes.fss:44`, `g(O, P)` with `P` a `Y[\2\]`, which no `n` meets, refused by the text. The test runs under walk only, so its verdict stays; the point is listed.

### Points the batch lists for you, not questions

- **Team lines changed:** walk's inference of a trait's generic method and its load check's messages (W); `LexicographicOrder`'s static parameters, `List`'s and `PureList`'s `extends` lines, the comment at `:3232`, and the checker's subtype case of a trait type, its trait and object declaration checks (X); the checker's dotted call, its arrow of a declaration, its trait-type check and its extender check (K).
- **What walk does differently:** a trait's generic dotted method takes the instance its object's own method takes, the `ZZ32` converted, its bound where nothing fixes it (W); an inherited generic functional method beside a plain one is chosen where only it fits (W, row 765); a refused generic pair names its rule (W). The library change moves no walk value (X).
- **What the checker does differently:** a list is ordered only where its elements are totally ordered (X); calls and types that break a `where` condition are refused where they were accepted, and a call that a `where`-clause variable can satisfy is accepted where it was refused (K).
- **Where a rung holds a line:** K, if one of its rows refuses a declaration of the compiler's own library; it lands the rest and reports.

\subsection{The traits that extend a closed trait}
\seclabel{revival-comprises}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-decls}; \secref{natparams}, by the
amendment of 9~October 2026.
\item[Change] The first sentence of a draft note in \secref{trait-decls},
which said that the traits listed in a \KWD{comprises} clause are exactly
the traits that immediately extend the declared trait and that they must
explicitly extend it, is replaced by normative text: every listed type
extends the declared trait \VAR{T}, and every value of type \VAR{T} is a
value of one of the listed types; a listed type may be an instantiation of
a parameterized trait whose static arguments contain no static variable
other than the static parameters of \VAR{T}; and a trait or object that explicitly extends
\VAR{T} is a subtype of a listed type, or a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause of its own each of whose listed types meets the same requirement, or
a trait with static parameters that at least one trait or object extends
and every trait or object extending it is a subtype of a listed type.
The note's second sentence, on a clause that includes ``\EXP{\ldots}'', is
kept in its note, and the example of \TYP{Molecule} is unchanged.
The new text answers the third question of Victor Luchangco's draft note
on trait identifiers earlier in the section, whether an instantiation of a
parameterized trait may be listed: it may.
An amendment of 9~October 2026 lets the static arguments of a listed type
contain a \KWD{where}-clause variable of the declaration of \VAR{T} as well,
the listed type then holding at every value of the variable, and adds one
sentence to \secref{natparams}: an argument whose type is a trait whose clause
lists a type at a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} \KWD{where}-clause variable, passed
where that listed type is expected with a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter in
the variable's place, instantiates that parameter, for that call, with the
size of the value itself, a size known to equal only itself.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
decided it on 28~September 2026.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) reads a \KWD{comprises}
clause as coverage: the clause ``specifies a set of types and generic types
determined by the generic type of the declaration'', and an instantiation of
the declared generic type ``is covered by the union of the types in this set
and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set'', one
generic type $G$ determining another $G'$ ``if every parameter of $G'$ is a
parameter of $G$''
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
277--283 and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
Welterweight Fortress, the calculus of the type group's paper of 2012
(Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, and Tristan, ``Dynamic
Dispatch and Type Inference Semipredicates''), reads it at the level of
values: ``no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of
the comprised types''; its rule for a trait declaration asks nothing of the
traits that extend a trait with such a clause
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick}, lines 38--62).
The draft note restated the rule of the compiled type checker of 2009,
under which \library\ could not close their marker of the integer types as
the team meant to: \TYP{AnyIntegral} lists the five integer types, and the
parameterized trait \EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}, which each
of them extends at itself, stands between them unlisted, as the team's
comment on the declaration records (``not yet: comprises
\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket} where
\EXP{\llbracket{}I\rrbracket}'', \nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi},
line 434).
\TYP{Integral} has a static parameter that \TYP{AnyIntegral} does not have,
so it can be listed only at particular static arguments, and every value of it is a value of one of the five.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-comprises/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The amendment follows the revival's default for the third question of its
array design, a size known only at run time, built on 9~October 2026 and
listed for the curator's review.
\library\ have carried on their trait \TYP{NatParam}, since 2007, the clause
``\EXP{\KWD{comprises}\;\{N\llbracket{}n\rrbracket\}\;\KWD{where}\;\llbracket\KWD{nat}\;n\rrbracket}''
as a comment, with the reading that a function taking an
\EXP{N\llbracket{}n\rrbracket} may be passed a \TYP{NatParam}, and ``within
that function n becomes a static nat parameter''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fss}, lines 15--26, in
the revival's repository).
The sentence of 28~September followed the Types chapter's rule by which one
generic type determines another, which does not consider \KWD{where}-clause
variables; \secref{where-clauses} allows a declaration to introduce them.
A size so opened is bound for the call, as inference binds a type parameter
to an argument's type, and since no program can write its name it cannot be
equal to a size written elsewhere.
The team wrote the same form at a type \KWD{where}-clause variable as a comment
on \TYP{AnyList} (``Not yet: comprises
\EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket} where \EXP{\llbracket{}E\rrbracket}'',
\nolinkurl{Library/List.fsi}, line 56, in the revival's repository); the
revival decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the
team wrote down, that comment among them.
The full reasoning of the amendment is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-size-expressions/REPORT.md} and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/array-fork3-judgement.md} in the revival's
repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker accepts the declaration of
\TYP{AnyIntegral} in \library\ as written
(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 433--436).
No example of this specification changes: \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule}, which
has no static parameters, is still not allowed.
The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
parameters over the declarations and object expressions it sees: a trait or object declared in
another component, below such a trait and a subtype of no listed type, is
not refused (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger). It compares the declarations it sees by their names: for a parameterized \VAR{T} its verdict can depend on how an extender spells its static parameters, and a trait or object that extends a trait of the same simple name in another API counts as an extender (rows~489 and~490).
It refuses an object expression that extends a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
clause, explicitly or through the traits it extends, and is a subtype of no
listed type, as the requirement on the trait's extenders together demands of
it, an object expression having neither static parameters nor a clause of its

input.new_string:
\appref{where-calculus} describes a Fortress core calculus with
\KWD{where} clauses.

An entry of an \KWD{extends} clause may carry a \KWD{where} clause of its
own (\secref{trait-decls}).
If that clause introduces no \KWD{where}-clause variable and all its
constraints are trait constraints, the declared trait or object extends the
entry's type exactly where the constraints hold:
an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type,
and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not.
Within the declaration the constraints hold: its \KWD{extends} clause and
its members are checked as if the constraints were in the declaration's own
\KWD{where} clause.
So a list is totally ordered exactly where its elements are:
%trait List[\E\] extends { ZeroIndexed[\E\],
%    LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] } }
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket \KWD{extends} \{\TYP{ZeroIndexed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{LexicographicOrder}\llbracket\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,E\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{E \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket\}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
\revision{revival-conditional}{This paragraph and its example are new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 gave each entry of an \KWD{extends}
clause an optional \KWD{where} clause in its grammar and stated no meaning
for it, and its front matter lists conditional extension among the
features not yet supported.}

A \KWD{where}-clause variable may not appear as a static argument

\chapter{Changes Since Fortress 1.0 Specifications}
\applabel{spec-changes}

\note{Changes Since
http://projectfortress.sun.com/Projects/Community/changeset/1444}

\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
\seclabel{revival-changes}
\sloppy

This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
open disagreement.
Each changed passage carries a box headed
``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.

Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
would require.
The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
there.
The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
Fortress~1.0 release.
The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
new one, is in the revival's decision records,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
and, for the number chapters,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
in the same repository.

Each change below follows a decision of the revival.
The first of those decisions, taken on
24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}, is that the compiled type checker keeps
the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
stated, and that the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
satisfy it.
An entry whose change does not follow from route~A says so, and names the
decision it follows or gives its reason.
The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
\secref{revival-routec}.

\item[Route C] The same under route~C, which places no type below
infinitely many instantiations of one trait.
\end{description}

\subsection{Conditional extension}
\seclabel{revival-conditional}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
\item[Change] A paragraph and an example are added, with a box: where the
\KWD{where} clause of an entry of an \KWD{extends} clause introduces no
\KWD{where}-clause variable and all its constraints are trait constraints,
the declared trait or object extends the entry's type exactly where the
constraints hold, and within the declaration the constraints hold while its
\KWD{extends} clause and its members are checked; the example is
\library's list, totally ordered exactly where its elements are.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the team
wrote down, among them that a trait that extends another under a
\KWD{where} condition is that type only where the condition holds and that
its members are checked under the condition, as Haskell checks an
instance's context, Rust a conditional implementation and Swift a
conditional conformance.
The grammar gives each entry of an \KWD{extends} clause its own optional
\KWD{where} clause, and the text orders lists ``whose elements support these
same comparison operators'' (\secref{comparisons-operators}), which no
unconditional declaration of the list type can state:
\library\ declared their list type as lexicographically ordered at every
element type, so the compiled type checker refused the comparison of two
elements of an unbounded type in the order's own body.
The team's internal notes foresaw conditional subtyping and its cost,
that ``we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular
method'' (\secref{internal-document}, in its subsection on wrapped fields
whose types are naked type variables).
A clause that introduces a \KWD{where}-clause variable, or whose
constraints are not all trait constraints, keeps the reading it had: the
entry is extended at every instance.
\library's list keeps an element-wise \EXP{=} of its own outside the
condition, so that a list whose elements are not ordered, a list of pairs
among them, is still compared element by element.
The alternative not taken is to read the clause as limiting nothing, the
extension holding at every instance, under which the clause has no effect
and the list's order needs another construct.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker reads such a clause as this
section says: a value of an instance whose static arguments satisfy the
constraints is of the entry's type, one whose static arguments do not is
refused where that type is expected, and the declaration's members and
\KWD{extends} clause are checked with the constraints holding.
\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
exactly where its elements are totally ordered.
It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{lexicographic-order} says
that such a list's order is partial: no partial lexicographic order of
lists is declared.
The compiled type checker still lets a member that it checked with the
constraints holding be called where they fail: it accepts a call of such
a member on an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them
(row~NEW-X-1 of the revival's gap ledger).
Its other readers of an \KWD{extends} clause, the members a type inherits
and its checks of the type hierarchy, read the entry as extended at every
instance.
The interpreter reads the extension as holding at every instance, and so
does the compiled run time: a type test of an instance whose static
arguments fail the constraints answers \VAR{true} on both
(row~NEW-X-2, gated for the interpreter by
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk.fss}),
so the interpreter keeps the order of a list of tuples or of floating-point
numbers.
The code generator compiles a declaration whose \KWD{extends} clause has
such a clause; it refuses one that carries a \KWD{where} clause of its own
(row~701).
\item[Original text] No such paragraph. The grammar is unchanged:
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 83,
\begin{quote}
\emph{TraitTypeWhere} ::= \emph{TraitType} \emph{Where}?
\end{quote}
and the front matter lists ``where clauses and conditional extension''
among the features not yet supported
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex}, line 82).
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

\subsection{The covariance example}

It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{lexicographic-order} says
that such a list's order is partial: no partial lexicographic order of
lists is declared.
The compiled type checker still lets a member that it checked with the
constraints holding be called where they fail: it accepts a call of such
a member on an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them
(row~NEW-X-1 of the revival's gap ledger).
Its other readers of an \KWD{extends} clause, the members a type inherits
and its checks of the type hierarchy, read the entry as extended at every
instance.
The interpreter reads the extension as holding at every instance, and so
does the compiled run time: a type test of an instance whose static
arguments fail the constraints answers \VAR{true} on both
(row~NEW-X-2, gated for the interpreter by
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk.fss}),
so the interpreter keeps the order of a list of tuples or of floating-point
numbers.
The code generator compiles a declaration whose \KWD{extends} clause has
such a clause; it refuses one that carries a \KWD{where} clause of its own
(row~701).
\item[Original text] No such paragraph. The grammar is unchanged:
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 83,
\begin{quote}
\emph{TraitTypeWhere} ::= \emph{TraitType} \emph{Where}?
\end{quote}
and the front matter lists ``where clauses and conditional extension''
among the features not yet supported
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex}, line 82).
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}
